No transition funding without measurable reductions, because unverified money would finance the same fires.

transcript.position: Indonesia opens by accepting that the 2015 haze was a regional emergency: Singapore's 24-hour PSI passed 300 and losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars [Background]. However, the cure is a funded domestic programme, not foreign jurisdiction. Indonesia therefore proposes that Indonesian courts and the Peatland Restoration Agency, created in January 2016 under Presidential Regulation 1/2016, handle every enforcement case on Indonesian soil. This works because the 2002 ASEAN Agreement already rests on sovereign control: Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right over its own resources, and Article 27 settles disputes by consultation, with no court or tribunal. A foreign statute that reaches conduct abroad, as Section 4 of Singapore's 2014 Act does, therefore goes beyond what all ten parties agreed.\n\nThe most damaging objection is that Indonesia is hiding behind sovereignty while the smoke keeps coming, especially with a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background]. Our answer is that we will share data in a form that works. Under Article 8(1) of the Agreement, fire and haze data already flows to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, so fire hotspot data can reach the monitoring system without releasing parcel-level concession maps. Those maps are restricted by domestic data law and overlap unresolved tenure disputes, so publishing them would create new conflicts, and under Section 8 of the Singapore Act a map supplied by a government could be used to presume liability against named owners in a foreign court. In return for a firm commitment to domestic enforcement and withheld maps, Indonesia will accept a moratorium with partial exemptions, applied by provincial administrations in phases. We cannot go further on the moratorium, because a full ban with no exemptions would fall on smallholders in the planting window with no alternative livelihood. A restriction on smallholders is only acceptable if a full donor fund pays for alternatives, because Indonesia cannot carry the transition cost alone. If Singapore and other ASEAN members fund the transition, Indonesia can move faster on peatland restoration.

key_claims.claim: ASEAN's own treaty gives no court or tribunal, so foreign courts ruling on acts on Indonesian soil go beyond what the parties agreed.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled by consultation or negotiation with no tribunal, and Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right to exploit its own resources, so an extraterritorial statute adds a remedy that the ten parties never accepted.

key_claims.claim: The Singapore Act's reach and liability presumption would turn Indonesian maps into evidence against landowners in a foreign court.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore, and Section 8 presumes that an owner or occupier of burning land caused the haze, with ownership provable from maps supplied by a foreign government, so releasing concession maps would feed claims of up to S$100,000 a day under Section 5(2)(a), capped at S$2 million under Section 5(5).

key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and it does not require parcel-level concession maps, which Indonesian data law restricts [Background].

transcript.position: We have moved since last round: Singapore now accepts district-level maps instead of full concession maps, a moratorium with partial exemptions, and a fully funded transition, and in return we hold firm on a joint ASEAN panel as the enforcement route. Indonesia's strongest point is that releasing parcel-level maps would hand a foreign court evidence under Section 8 of our Act, where an owner of burning land is presumed to have caused the haze and liability runs at up to S$100,000 a day [S2]. We answer that district maps remove that fear, because they name no parcel owner, yet they still let the panel match fire hotspots reported under Article 8(1) [S1] to a district and a permit class. Because the panel, not a Singapore court, would then decide which cases go further, Indonesia keeps control of its land data and the aggregate fine cap stays at S$2 million [S2 s5(5)]. We also concede on money: Indonesia says a restriction on smallholders is acceptable only if alternatives are funded, and that is a fair point, since a moratorium with no livelihood alternative would push people back to burning. If Indonesia accepts the joint panel, Singapore will support a full donor fund, but every tranche is released only against measured falls in hotspots and PSI days, because unverified money would finance the same fires. The fund would be governed by a donor board that includes Indonesia's Peatland Restoration Agency, and who besides Singapore pays must be settled with other ASEAN members and donors, as no figure for their shares is established in our sources.\n\nThe most damaging objection to our package is that Article 27 gives ASEAN no tribunal, so a panel has no legal footing [S1]. Our answer is that Article 27 requires consultation and negotiation, so the panel would be created by consent of the parties as a consultation body that reviews evidence and recommends, not as a court, and therefore needs no foreign jurisdiction over Indonesian soil. On the Section 6 private right to sue, Singapore would defer its use for any fire the panel is already reviewing, while keeping it for cases the panel declines or leaves unresolved, because Singapore residents who suffered the 2015 episode, with PSI above 300 [Background], cannot be left with no remedy. We cannot go below an attribution mechanism, since otherwise the next dry season, with a greater than 90% chance of El Nino lasting through winter [Background], repeats with no one answerable.

key_claims.claim: District-level maps give attribution at far lower tenure and data-law risk than parcel-level maps, so they bridge the gap between us.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 8 presumes the owner or occupier of burning land caused the haze and allows proof from maps supplied by a foreign government, so district maps, which name no parcel owner, avoid the exposure Indonesia fears while [S1] Article 8(1) hotspot data can still be matched to districts.

key_claims.claim: A consent-based joint panel needs no tribunal and no foreign court, so it fits within the treaty's consultation model.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 settles disputes by consultation or negotiation, and a panel created by the parties' agreement is an extension of consultation, while [S2] Section 4's extraterritorial reach, which Indonesia rejects, is held back for cases the panel handles.

key_claims.claim: A fully funded transition with verified reductions answers Indonesia's smallholder concern at low cost to Singapore's interests.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] Regional losses in 2015 ran into the tens of billions of dollars and PSI passed 300, so paying for alternatives against measured hotspot and PSI-day reductions is cheaper than another episode, and [S2] Section 5(5) caps fines at S$2 million, which could never recover such losses.

key_claims.evidence: [Background] The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gives a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter, so exemptions should not cover peatland that is burning or drained in the coming dry season.

transcript.position: We have moved since round one: Indonesia now accepts a moratorium with no exemptions and district-level concession maps, and in return we hold firm on Indonesian courts and a fully funded transition. Singapore's strongest point is that without ownership data a repeat of the 2015 haze, when PSI passed 300 [Background], cannot be traced to any owner. We accept that need, so Indonesia offers concession maps aggregated by district, shared with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System. This lets the monitoring system match hotspots to districts and lets Indonesian agencies identify the companies, while parcel boundaries stay protected by domestic data law and unresolved tenure disputes. Parcel-level release would be risky because Section 8 of Singapore's Act presumes that an owner or occupier of burning land caused the haze, and lets ownership be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government [S2]. District data cuts that risk, and it still goes beyond the hotspot reporting required by Article 8(1) of the ASEAN Agreement [S1].\n\nOn enforcement, Singapore says the joint panel is gentler than its own Act. However, Article 27 of the Agreement provides only consultation and no tribunal [S1], so a panel with power to rule on cases on Indonesian soil would need new legal authority that no party has agreed, and that would cross our red line against foreign jurisdiction. Indonesian courts and the Peatland Restoration Agency will therefore handle every case, and we will give the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre a written report on each hotspot case, so Singapore can see outcomes. The most damaging objection is that Indonesian courts alone are not credible. Our answer is that the reports and the tranche verification described below put the results in public view. In return for Indonesian-only enforcement, Singapore can leave the private right to sue under Section 6 of its Act untouched for harm in Singapore, as we do not ask it to be waived, but it would not be applied to concessions already prosecuted in Indonesia. On the moratorium, we give Singapore the full version it wants, because it is the issue that matters least to us and most to them. This is conditional on a full donor fund, because Indonesia has limited fiscal capacity, and a ban on smallholders in the planting window without funded alternatives is a red line. We accept Singapore's idea that money is released in tranches against measured hotspot and PSI reductions, with a fund governed jointly by donors and Indonesia and verified by hotspot data. Singapore has offered only partial funding and has not named other donors, so we ask all ASEAN members and other donors to contribute, which spreads the cost. Paying for the transition is cheaper than another season like 2015, with losses in the tens of billions of dollars [Background], and El Nino conditions with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter make delay dangerous.

transcript.position:
We have moved since last round: Singapore now accepts the full moratorium with no exemptions that Indonesia offered, and keeps district-level maps and a full donor fund, so the one issue we still hold is a joint ASEAN panel on enforcement. Indonesia's strongest point is that a panel with power over cases on Indonesian soil would exceed Article 27 of the 2002 Agreement, which provides only consultation and no tribunal [S1]. We answer by shrinking the panel to fit that limit: Indonesian courts and the Peatland Restoration Agency keep first-instance handling of every case, and the panel only reviews the written case reports Indonesia has offered to send the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre and publishes recommendations. It has no power to rule or fine on Indonesian land, so no foreign jurisdiction is created. In return, Singapore takes the tighter moratorium Indonesia says it cares least about and agrees to the full donor fund it asked for. Both moves cost us little and give Indonesia its two stated priorities of funded smallholders and control of its land.

The most damaging objection to our own package is the one the judge noted: a district map names no owner, so how does it support attribution? The answer is that the district map matches a hotspot to an area, and Indonesia's own written case report, which it has already offered, must name the concession holder identified by its agencies for each hotspot case. The panel can then check that the named company holds a permit in that district. Singapore does not need parcel maps for this, and the Section 8 presumption in our Act [S2] would only be used for harm in Singapore after a case is left unresolved. On funding risk, we propose that tranches be measured on hotspot counts adjusted for El Nino conditions rather than raw PSI days, because a greater than 90% chance of El Nino lasting through the northern winter [Background] means weather could otherwise penalise Indonesia for fires it cannot control. If a tranche is withheld, the smallholder alternative payments are paid first and ring-fenced, so farmers are not punished for a missed target. If donors fall short, the moratorium on smallholder plots is phased in by province as funded, while the ban on company concessions applies at once. Singapore will not fund without measured reductions, but we accept this fairer measurement.

key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 settles disputes by consultation or negotiation, and a panel that only reviews Indonesia's own case reports and recommends is an extension of consultation, while Indonesian courts keep every first-instance case.

key_claims.claim: District maps plus Indonesia's named-concession case reports give workable attribution without parcel maps.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) already requires hotspot data to flow to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, and Indonesia's offered written report per case adds the identified company, so hotspots matched to a district can be tied to an owner, whereas [S2] Section 8 would apply only to unresolved harm in Singapore.

key_claims.claim: Funding tranches should use El Nino-adjusted hotspot counts and ring-fence smallholder payments, so Indonesia is not penalised for weather and farmers are protected if a tranche is withheld.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gives a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the northern winter, and PSI passed 300 in 2015 [Background], so raw PSI days would mix weather with enforcement.

key_claims.claim: Paying for a full moratorium and full fund is far cheaper than another season like 2015.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] Regional losses in 2015 ran into the tens of billions of dollars, while [S2] Section 5(5) caps Singapore's aggregate fine at S$2 million, so fines could never recover such losses.

concessions: If Indonesia accepts a review-only joint ASEAN panel, Singapore accepts a moratorium with no exemptions, as Indonesia offered.
If Indonesia accepts the panel and the named-company case reports, Singapore accepts district-level maps and drops parcel-level maps.
Singapore supports a full donor fund, with tranches measured on El Nino-adjusted hotspot counts and smallholder payments ring-fenced.
Singapore defers its own Act and Section 6 private suits for any case Indonesian courts have prosecuted and the panel has reviewed.

transcript.position: We have moved on enforcement since last round: Indonesia will accept a joint ASEAN panel, but only as a consent-based consultation body that reviews evidence and recommends, while Indonesian courts and the Peatland Restoration Agency alone decide and enforce cases on Indonesian soil. The judge was right that I treated the panel as binding, and Singapore has said it would recommend, not rule. On that basis the panel fits Article 27 of the 2002 Agreement, which provides for consultation and negotiation and no tribunal [S1], and it does not cross our red line against foreign jurisdiction. In return we need three things. Singapore must defer its own Act and Section 6 private suits for any fire the panel is reviewing, because Section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore and Section 8 presumes the owner of burning land caused the haze [S2]. Singapore must also confirm the full donor fund. And the moratorium should carry partial exemptions, which Singapore has already offered, so that smallholders are not cut off in the planting window.\n\nThe most damaging objection is the one the judge raised: district maps name no owner, so how can a case be built? Our answer is that the panel flags a hotspot in a district and permit class using Article 8(1) data [S1]. The Indonesian agencies then identify the permit holder from the parcel registry under domestic data law and report the result to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre case by case, so no parcel data leaves Indonesia and no foreign court receives maps under Section 8 [S2]. On money, tranches must track measured hotspot reductions, but PSI days must be adjusted for weather, because El Nino has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background] and Indonesia should not lose funds for drought it cannot control. If donors fund less than in full, the moratorium's phased provincial rollout shrinks to match the money received, because no restriction may fall on smallholders without funded alternatives. This is a package Singapore has itself proposed, so we can close it now, before the dry season, when haze like the 2015 episode with PSI above 300 [Background] is most likely.

key_claims.claim: A consent-based panel that only recommends is compatible with the treaty and leaves decisions with Indonesian courts, so it does not breach our sovereignty line.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 settles disputes by consultation or negotiation with no tribunal, so a panel created by the parties' consent and limited to reviewing evidence and recommending adds no foreign jurisdiction over Indonesian soil.

key_claims.claim: District maps can still support attribution because Indonesian agencies, not foreign courts, link a flagged district and permit class to a permit holder.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires fire and haze data to be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, and [S2] Section 8 allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, which is the exposure that district-level maps avoid.

key_claims.claim: Singapore must defer its own Act for fires under panel review, otherwise the panel adds a second layer of liability on top of the statute.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 5(2)(a) allows fines of up to S$100,000 per day, capped at S$2 million in aggregate under Section 5(5), and Section 6 allows private suits whether or not the conduct is actionable abroad.

key_claims.claim: Tranches must be weather-adjusted and the moratorium must scale to the money actually received, so that smallholders are not penalised for drought or donor shortfalls.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gives a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter, and regional losses in 2015 ran into the tens of billions of dollars, so funded and fair verification is cheaper than another episode.

concessions: If Singapore defers its Act and Section 6 suits for fires under panel review and confirms a full donor fund, Indonesia accepts a joint ASEAN panel as a recommending consultation body.
If the panel stays advisory and Indonesian courts decide cases, Indonesia shares concession maps aggregated by district with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System.
If the fund is full, Indonesia accepts a moratorium with partial exemptions that are time-limited and exclude peatland that is burning or drained.
Indonesia accepts tranche release against measured hotspot reductions and will send the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre a written report on each case.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: the panel may only consult and recommend, and Indonesian courts alone decide and enforce.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: if donors fund less than in full, the phased moratorium shrinks to match the money received.

scores.justification: Full parcel-level maps, a new joint ASEAN panel and a no-exemption moratorium all need Indonesian consent. Indonesia has already refused the maps on sovereignty and data-law grounds. Article 27 of the treaty provides no tribunal, so the panel would need a new legal basis, which Singapore does not explain. Tranche-based funding tied to hotspot and PSI reductions is workable in principle.

It names each package element, gives the fine figures (S$100,000 per day, S$2 million cap) and ties funding tranches to hotspot and PSI reductions. It sets no numeric thresholds, no donor fund size and no panel composition.

It admits Indonesia's sovereignty objection and that Singapore cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia. It offers to hold back its own Act and to drop the demand for full funding. It does not discuss the cost to smallholders or existing permit holders of a no-exemption moratorium, and it does not discuss what releasing full maps costs Indonesia in tenure conflicts.

There are no earlier statements to contradict. The package follows directly from the opening principle that whoever burns must be identifiable. The offered concessions and red lines match the package.

It anticipates Indonesia's sovereignty and extraterritoriality objections and answers them with Article 3(1) and the joint panel. It also offers to hold back the Act where the panel is already handling a case. It does not yet address data-law or tenure-dispute concerns, because no Indonesian argument had been made.

judgments.summary: Singapore proposes full concession maps shared with the regional monitoring system, a joint ASEAN panel for attribution and enforcement, a moratorium with no exemptions, and partial donor funding released only against measured reductions in hotspots and bad-air days. In return it would hold back its own law for cases the panel is already handling and would not press for full funding. The argument is coherent and specific, but it leans on a stretched reading of the treaty's data duty. It also says little about the burden on smallholders and permit holders.
unsupported_claims: Article 8(1) is presented as an existing duty to share concession maps. It covers fire and haze data, not parcel-level ownership maps.
'Prevention is far cheaper than penalty' has no cost figures behind it. The sources only give the S$2 million cap and 'tens of billions' in regional losses.
The claim that a joint ASEAN panel is a less intrusive fit with the treaty has no source. Nothing in the sources provides for or mentions such a panel.

scores.justification: Indonesian courts and a phased provincial moratorium use existing institutions. But the plan depends on a full donor fund that no donor has agreed to. It also asks Singapore to give up attribution entirely, which leaves little room for agreement. The Peatland Restoration Agency is described as handling enforcement, which stretches its role of restoration.

It names the package, the Agency, Presidential Regulation 1/2016 and the phased provincial approach. It gives no fund amount, no timeline for phasing, no enforcement caseload commitment and no reporting intervals beyond 'as agreed'.

It admits the haze was a regional emergency and that Indonesia cannot carry the transition cost alone. It does not say what withheld maps and domestic-only enforcement cost Singapore, namely no way to attribute or pursue owners. It does not say what exemptions cost in continued fire risk.

The package matches its stated sovereignty and smallholder red lines. There is one tension: it says hotspot data 'already flows' under Article 8(1), yet it makes the same reporting conditional on a full donor fund.

It pre-empts the charge of hiding behind sovereignty. It engages Section 8 and Section 4 of Singapore's Act directly and explains why parcel-level maps would become evidence against owners. It offers hotspot data as an alternative. It does not address how attribution would work without maps.

judgments.summary: Indonesia proposes that Indonesian courts and its restoration agency handle all enforcement, that concession maps be withheld, that the moratorium carry partial exemptions applied in phases by provinces, and that donors fully fund the transition. It would share hotspot data through the existing treaty channel. It relies on the treaty's lack of a tribunal and on Singapore's liability presumption to justify withholding maps. It makes some concessions on the moratorium, but its core demands leave no attribution mechanism, and some supporting facts are unsupported.
unsupported_claims: The >90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter, attributed to a 13 August 2015 ENSO discussion, does not appear in the scenario or in the listed sources.
'All ten parties' is not in the scenario or sources. Neither gives the number of parties to the Agreement.
The maps 'overlap unresolved tenure disputes' is not supported. The scenario only says Indonesia cited sovereignty and domestic data law.
The Peatland Restoration Agency is said to handle 'every enforcement case'. The sources describe it as a peatland restoration body, not an enforcement authority.
The claim that the moratorium falls on smallholders in a 'planting window' has no supporting source.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Neither side addresses whether a joint ASEAN panel needs treaty amendment or new legal authority, given that Article 27 provides no tribunal.
Neither side says what happens to Singapore residents' private right to sue under Section 6 of the Act, whether it is kept, waived or deferred under any package.
Neither side addresses how credible enforcement would be under Indonesian courts alone, including capacity and independence of the courts.
Neither side considers the middle option of maps aggregated by district, or whether it could allow attribution with fewer tenure and data-law problems.
Neither side addresses compensation or legal challenge by existing permit holders if the moratorium has no exemptions, or how exemptions would affect fire risk in the next dry season.
Neither side says who besides Singapore would pay into a donor fund, or how a fund would be governed and verified.
Neither side addresses the interim risk if no deal is reached before the next dry season.

scores.justification: A consent-based joint panel as a consultation body that recommends fits Article 27, and the donor board including the Peatland Restoration Agency is workable. Weakened because who besides Singapore pays is admitted as unsettled and the panel's power is thin.

Names district maps, S$100,000/day and S$2m cap, tranches tied to hotspot and PSI days, deferral of Section 6 suits for fires under panel review. No fund size, panel composition or time limit on exemptions.

Admits no donor-share figure is established and concedes smallholder livelihood costs. But it barely admits what the panel and retained Section 6 suits cost Indonesia, or that a recommend-only panel may not deliver attribution.
Opens with 'We have moved' and explains each shift (district maps, partial exemptions, full fund) as conditional on the panel. Red lines on attribution and verified money are unchanged.
Answers Indonesia's Section 8 fear with district maps, takes up the smallholder/funded-alternatives point, and rebuts the Article 27 no-tribunal objection directly.

judgments.summary: Singapore dropped parcel-level maps for district-level ones, accepted partial exemptions and a full donor fund, and kept a joint ASEAN panel as the enforcement route. It described the panel as a consent-based consultation body that reviews evidence and recommends. It would defer its own Act and private suits for fires the panel is reviewing, but keeps them for cases the panel declines. Its weak points are that the panel's authority is thin and the funding shares are undefined.
unsupported_claims: The ENSO 13 August 2015 'greater than 90% chance' is cited to [Background], not the listed sources; the dry season it refers to is the 2015-16 winter, but Singapore applies it to 'the next dry season', which is a stretch.
Claim that partial exemptions 'reduce legal challenge risk' has no support in the scenario or sources.

scores.justification: District maps, written reports on each case to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre and tranche funding are doable. A full ban with no exemptions, phased by provinces, and a full donor fund with unnamed donors are less certain given the fiscal limits it admits.
Gives district maps to the monitoring system, a written report per hotspot case, tranche release against hotspot and PSI measures, and joint fund governance. No amounts, timelines or phase schedule.

Concedes parcel release is risky and that courts alone lack credibility, and notes it gives up the moratorium it values least. It does not admit the cost to Singapore of losing a panel, or of keeping a Section 6 right that is unused for prosecuted concessions.

Opens with 'We have moved' and explains shifts on maps and the moratorium as trades for courts-only and a full fund. Red lines on foreign jurisdiction and smallholders hold. Round 1 said it could not go further than partial exemptions, and the reversal is framed as a concession and explained.

Takes up Singapore's attribution point, rebuts the panel on Article 27, answers the 'courts not credible' objection with public reports, and notes Singapore offered only partial funding. It does not engage Singapore's consultation-body framing of the panel.

judgments.summary: Indonesia now offers district-level maps and a moratorium with no exemptions. It holds firm on Indonesian courts only and a full donor fund. It argues a panel with power over cases on Indonesian soil would exceed Article 27, and offers written reports on each hotspot case and tranche verification instead. It asks all ASEAN members and other donors to share the cost. Its weakness is that it treats Singapore's panel as binding when Singapore proposed a recommending body.
unsupported_claims: It says Singapore 'has offered only partial funding', which is outdated; Singapore's round 2 text accepts a full fund. The claim reflects round 1 only.
Claim that district data 'goes beyond the hotspot reporting required by Article 8(1)' is plausible but Article 8(1) does not state it either way.
That the planting window is near and that Indonesia has limited fiscal capacity are cited to [Background], which does not contain them.
The El Nino 90% figure is cited to [Background] but it concerns the 2015-16 winter, not now.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Neither side addressed who bears the cost if donors refuse to fund in full, and what happens to the moratorium and smallholders if the fund falls short.

Neither addressed how district-level maps can support attribution when they name no owner; a company cannot be identified from a district and permit class, and no one explained how the Section 8 presumption or any case could work.
Neither explained how the moratorium would be enforced against fires in the coming dry season while the fund and panel are still being set up.
Neither addressed what happens to smallholders and communities who lose income if tranches are withheld because hotspots do not fall.
Neither addressed the risk that tying tranches to PSI days penalises Indonesia for haze caused by weather such as El Nino or by fires outside its control.

scores.justification: Review-only panel using Indonesia's own case reports, plus ring-fenced smallholder payments and province-by-province phasing when donors fall short, are workable. Weak point: no donor commitments are named and the fund's size and payers are left open.

Concrete mechanisms: El Nino-adjusted hotspot counts, smallholder payments paid first, company ban applying at once, and a panel that checks the named company holds a permit in that district. No fund amounts, tranche sizes or panel membership.

It admits the weather risk to Indonesia and the risk to farmers if a tranche is withheld. It calls the full moratorium and full fund 'cost us little' and says little about what the panel review and the retained Section 8 and Section 6 rights cost Indonesia.

It says it has moved: it now accepts the full moratorium and drops the partial exemptions it proposed last round. It keeps the district maps, the panel and the full fund, and it keeps the red lines on attribution and measured reductions. The one change is explained as a response to Indonesia's offer.

It takes on Indonesia's Article 27 objection by shrinking the panel to review and recommend. It answers the district-map attribution objection using Indonesia's offered case reports. It adopts Indonesia's weather-adjustment concern. It does not address Indonesia's demand that Section 6 be deferred while the panel reviews a fire, beyond a narrower deferral for prosecuted cases.

judgments.summary: Singapore gives way on the moratorium by accepting the full version with no exemptions, and it keeps district maps, the full donor fund and a review-only joint panel. It shrinks the panel to fit Article 27, and it ties attribution to Indonesia's own named-company case reports. It adds weather-adjusted tranches and ring-fenced smallholder payments, and it phases the smallholder ban in by province as donors fund it. It still holds back Section 8 and Section 6 for cases left unresolved.
unsupported_claims: It says it 'accepts the full moratorium ... that Indonesia offered', but Indonesia's round 3 text moved to partial exemptions. This appears to rely on Indonesia's earlier position, not its latest one.

It claims the Section 8 presumption would only be used after a case is left unresolved. Section 8 as quoted contains no such limit, so this is a Singapore policy choice, not something the source supports.
The statement that Indonesia's case report 'must name the concession holder' is not supported by Article 8(1), which covers hotspot data only. The report is a voluntary Indonesian offer.

scores.justification: A recommending panel, agency-run attribution from the parcel registry, weather-adjusted tranches and a phased rollout sized to the money received can all be carried out. The partial exemptions depend on donors paying in full, and the 'close it now' timetable is optimistic.

Gives clear conditions: Singapore defers its Act and Section 6 for fires under panel review, a case-by-case report goes to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, exemptions are time-limited and exclude burning or drained peatland, and the rollout scales to funding received. It gives no fund amounts or deadlines.

It concedes that it wrongly treated the panel as binding. It admits donor shortfalls shrink the moratorium. It does not say what district maps, exemptions and deferral of Singapore's remedies cost Singapore or the haze-affected public.

It explicitly flags the move to accepting the panel as a recommending body, and ties it to the judge's earlier point. But it also reverses on the moratorium, from no exemptions to partial exemptions, and that change is framed as 'already offered by Singapore'. Its earlier statement that the moratorium matters least to it sits awkwardly with the reversal.

It engages Singapore's review-only panel, the attribution question, and the Singapore idea of weather adjustment. It asks Singapore for a deferral of its Act and Section 6 suits. It does not engage Singapore's red line on funding conditions beyond accepting measured reductions.

judgments.summary: Indonesia now accepts a consent-based joint panel that only reviews and recommends, with Indonesian courts alone deciding cases. It accepts district maps and answers the attribution question by having its own agencies name the permit holder from the parcel registry. It asks Singapore to defer its Act and Section 6 suits for fires under panel review and to confirm the full fund. It reverses its previous offer of a moratorium with no exemptions and asks for time-limited partial exemptions, and it asks for the moratorium to scale down if donors fund less than in full.
unsupported_claims: It says partial exemptions are 'already offered' by Singapore. Singapore's round 3 text withdrew that offer and accepted a full moratorium.
It claims Section 5(2)(a) and Section 5(5) show the panel adds a second layer of liability. The cited sections concern fines and caps and say nothing about a panel.
The statement that Indonesian agencies can identify permit holders from the parcel registry under domestic data law is an Indonesian assertion, and no listed source supports it.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Who pays the full donor fund and how large it is: neither side names a figure or any donor beyond a general appeal to ASEAN members.

If Indonesia's own case reports are the only route to naming owners, what happens when reports are late, incomplete or name no company? Neither side says what the panel does then, or who judges the reports' credibility.
Haze-affected Singapore residents lose time or remedy if Section 6 suits are deferred for fires under panel review. Neither side sets a time limit on the review.
Weather-adjusting tranches could let real fires pass as El Nino effects. Neither side specifies who sets the adjustment or how to prevent gaming.

Phasing the smallholder moratorium to the money received could leave large areas of peatland unrestricted in the coming dry season, with a greater than 90% El Nino chance. Neither side addresses the resulting fire risk.
The panel has no basis in the treaty beyond Article 27 consultation. Neither side addresses its membership, procedure, cost or who creates it.

recommendation.headline: Give up district-level maps and a donor-fund share to get named-company attribution and payment only for measured haze cuts

options.condition: Indonesia accepts a review-only panel and offers written case reports naming the permit holder for each hotspot case
options.action: Singapore defers its Act and Section 6 suits only for cases under panel review, with a fixed review deadline; it resumes them if no named-company report arrives.
options.requires_concession: Singapore delays its own legal remedy, and affected residents wait, during panel review.
options.principal_risk: Late or vague Indonesian reports could stall attribution, and no source sets the review time limit.

options.condition: Indonesia asks for time-limited partial exemptions on the moratorium and a full donor fund
options.action: Accept partial exemptions that exclude burning or drained peatland, and release Singapore's money in tranches tied to weather-adjusted hotspot reductions, smallholder payments first.
options.requires_concession: Singapore accepts a weaker moratorium and commits to a donor fund of unspecified size.
options.principal_risk: Exemptions and funding-linked phasing could leave peatland open in a dry season with a greater than 90% El Nino chance, and weather adjustment could be gamed.

options.condition: Indonesia refuses any attribution route, whether through district maps, case reports or a panel, and insists on Indonesian courts alone with no reporting
options.action: Withhold Singapore's funding and keep the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in force; do not sign a deal without an attribution mechanism.
options.requires_concession: Singapore forgoes a deal, the funding link and cooperation gains for this dry season.
options.principal_risk: The Act's extraterritorial reach is untested and Singapore cannot compel enforcement in Indonesia, so haze could recur with no deal in place.

recommendation.rationale: Indonesian plantation companies and the fires on their land cause the haze, so the Indonesian government and those companies should bear the clean-up and restoration costs; Singapore should co-fund only against verified reductions, since it suffers the PSI exposure. District maps name no owner, so attribution depends on Indonesia's agencies naming the permit holder; that is why the deferral of our Act is tied to those reports arriving.
recommendation.plain_summary: Offer to accept district-level maps, a review-only joint panel and funding released in tranches, and to defer our Act for cases under review. In return, ask Indonesia's agencies to name the permit holder in each fire case, so attribution survives and our money follows measured reductions.

recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (4): The options track the zone of agreement in rounds 2-3. Both sides had converged on a review-only panel, district maps, case reports naming the permit holder, tranche funding and time-limited partial exemptions. The conditions are concrete. The fixed review deadline has no source and the fund size is unspecified, and the recommendation admits both gaps.

Trade-off coverage (4): It covers attribution versus sovereignty, the cost of deferring the Act and Section 6 suits, a weaker moratorium in an El Niño dry season, funding conditionality, weather adjustment, and the untested extraterritorial reach. It leaves out who besides Singapore pays, and how the fund is governed. It also says nothing on phasing the moratorium to match funding received, or on the fallback if donors fall short.

Priority consistency (4): Both red lines hold. Attribution is the condition for the deferral, and funding is released only against verified reductions. The walk-away option protects the attribution red line. The headline "give up district-level maps and a donor-fund share" does not match the opening package, which has district maps and a partial fund. The rationale's claim that Indonesian companies should bear the costs sits awkwardly with the offer of a full donor fund in option 2.

Counterpart consideration (3): Smallholder payments come first, partial exemptions are accepted, and a review-only panel respects the Article 27 limit. The recommendation never says that Indonesian courts decide cases. It does not treat the data-law and tenure concerns as Indonesia's interests. Nor does it address Indonesia's insistence that Singapore's Act be deferred more broadly. Indonesia's red lines are largely implicit.

Strong arguments (4): It uses the debate's best points. District maps do not name an owner, so Indonesian case reports must. The deferral is tied to receiving those reports. Tranches are adjusted for weather and smallholders are paid first. It also keeps the Act as the fallback. The Section 8 presumption and the S$2m cap are not used.

Options (3 listed, 3 distinct): a conditional deal on attribution, a deal on moratorium and funding, and a walk-away. The third is a fallback rather than a negotiated option, but it differs in substance from the first two.

Package is fairly aggressive (full maps, no exemptions), but the concessions offered are credible.
